title: Why Houses Became Unaffordable (And Who's Buying Them)
alts: Houses Cost 5 Years of Income Now. Here's Why.
Is Wall Street Buying All the Houses? Housing Crisis Explained
line1: Why are houses so unaffordable? In 1995 a home cost ~3 years of income. Today it's almost 5. Here's what changed, and who's really buying.
summary: Dave's dad bought a house in 1995 on one salary. Dave and his partner can't, even with two. We compare home prices and incomes then and now (NAR, Census), explain why 7% mortgage rates hurt so much, how cheap pandemic mortgages created the lock-in effect, why America is short about 3.7 to 3.8 million homes, how zoning, permits and building costs slow construction, how much Wall Street investors really own (small nationally, big in Atlanta), and why the typical first-time buyer is now 40. This is the final episode of Series 3.
learn: How home prices compare to incomes in 1995 vs 2026 (about 3.2 vs 4.9 years)
Why today's ~7% mortgage rates make monthly payments so much bigger
What the mortgage rate lock-in effect is and why fewer homes are for sale
How big the U.S. housing shortage is and why builders can't just build more
How much institutional investors really own, nationally and in cities like Atlanta
Why the first-time buyer age hit 40, and rent vs buy tips (education, not advice)
